newsitem.title: BURMA: Some students leave Burma's troubled universities.
newsitem.headline: Some students leave Burma's troubled universities.

text.p: Hundreds of boarding students at two troubled universities left for home after protests in central Rangoon by their colleagues, campus sources said on Sunday.
About one third of 2,275 boarding students at the Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) had left their sprawling campus for the provinces since midweek, they told Reuters.
At the University of Yangon (Rangoon), about half of its boarding students had also chosen to leave before normal school holidays due in two months, the sources said.
Details of numbers leaving were unavailable.
The student exodus was prompted by fears that the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) might close down universities in reprisal for the protests, they added.
One of the student demands at the two protests last week was that they do not close down institutions of higher learning.
Earlier this week a government spokesman told Reuters that the authorities had no plans to close them down. However, the SLORC has not said how it will address student demands.

Last week up to 2,000 students staged the biggest street demonstration seen in the capital since the student-led pro-democracy uprising of September 1988. The military crushed that uprising, leaving thousands dead or in prison.
Over 500 students held another protest on Friday which soldiers and police broke up using water cannon and batons.
A total of over 860 students were held after the two major protests and later freed.

Among other demands, the students want to be allowed to set up student unions and have asked the official media to publish details of alleged poice brutality against some of their colleagues during a brawl with restaurant owners in October.

They had also sought more freedom and human rights and said their protest had no links with a pro-democracy movement led by opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi or her National League for Democracy Party.
The YIT and other universities were closed for extended periods after the 1988 uprising.
YIT and the University of Yangon authorities said they had not announced any closure but they had given students the option of leaving for their own safety.
"We have not officially announced a closure of the campus. Its up to the students to decide whether to go home," one campus source said.
There has been speculation among students and members of the public that many educational institutes might announce closures soon as a result of the student disturbances.
They said campus officials had assisted students to travel back to their provinces by arranging air, bus and train tickets.
The boarding students left before their final examinations this year. The tests are due in February.
